splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing for selecting actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA's multiemployer pension provisions. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running and the court retains authority to revoke after the nominal expiration date.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled by absconding because the statute does not authorize judicial tolling, and the term expires as stated in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions; they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects whether election-rule disputes can be addressed before elections or must be funneled into post-election litigation.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly affect the integrity of the vote count, including laws extending ballot-receipt deadlines.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election rules without showing a concrete, particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in criminal contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity. The issue has gained significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions that expand criminal liability, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal sentences.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that when the Sentencing Commission's commentary interprets an ambiguous Guideline, courts should defer to the Commission's interpretation even if it expands criminal liability, rather than applying lenity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (requiring only one).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or whether meeting any one is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses nationwide.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) encompasses inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether Application Note 1 to the career-offender guideline, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to Stinson deference or impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects thousands of career-offender designations annually.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid and controls
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to deference under Stinson, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses.

positions.label: Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b)'s text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot add what the text omits, so conspiracy does not qualify as a controlled substance offense under the career-offender guideline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state controls a substance not listed on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the underlying substance to be controlled under federal law, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include any offense under state law, without requiring the substance to also be federally controlled.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that the state conviction must involve a substance also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act to qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violating conditions of supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the seriousness of the violation conduct and other § 3553(a) factors without punitive intent.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to explicitly impose punitive sentences at supervised release revocation, while other circuits hold that revocation is not meant to punish the original offense or the violation itself. This affects hundreds of revocation sentences annually.

positions.label: Courts may expressly punish at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose sentences at supervised release revocation that explicitly serve a punitive purpose, permitting courts to punish defendants for their violations.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should not be punitive
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is not to punish the defendant but to sanction the violation and address the need for further supervision or incarceration based on the violation's nature.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing such relief exceeds the Commission's authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law (particularly the First Step Act's § 924(c) anti-stacking amendment) can serve as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits have held they cannot, while other circuits and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement allow consideration of such changes.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission cannot override this through policy statements.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as part of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, particularly under the Sentencing Commission's amended policy statement U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert their Chapter 13 case to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This affects debtors' ability to retain equity gains when circumstances force conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad definition of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) limits the converted estate to property as valued at the time of the original petition filing, so post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal of an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view applying the civil deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline (30 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline (14 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case and the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody (such as First Step Act time credit calculations) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may bring a civil rights action or other statutory claim.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging decisions that affect the fact or duration of confinement (such as BOP denials of earned time credits under the First Step Act), or whether Bivens/civil rights actions are also available. This split has deepened with First Step Act earned-time-credit disputes.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration of custody, including First Step Act time credit denials, must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus under § 2241.

positions.label: Both habeas and civil rights actions available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may pursue either habeas corpus or civil rights claims when challenging conditions or terms of confinement, depending on the nature of the relief sought.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Carmona v. U.S. Bureau of Prisons

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court's denial of a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical information qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order.' Other circuits have not uniformly recognized such orders as immediately appealable, creating a potential split on the scope of the collateral order doctrine for privacy-related sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that warrants immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are interlocutory and not immediately appealable because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have disagreed on the standards for evaluating discrimination liability and available remedies in hospitality, retail, and other service industries. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach to these legal questions, suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards for fair treatment and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies broader standards for establishing discrimination claims in business establishments, potentially allowing more claims to proceed.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, requiring a higher threshold for liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a trademark owner asserting likelihood of confusion must demonstrate that consumers are likely to be confused at the time of purchase, or whether post-sale confusion experienced by third-party observers is sufficient to support a trademark infringement claim.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether post-sale confusion — confusion experienced by observers who did not themselves purchase the product — can independently support a trademark infringement claim, or whether the relevant confusion must occur at the point of sale.

positions.label: Post-sale confusion is sufficient
positions.summary: Holds that likelihood of confusion is not limited to the point of sale and that confusion among third-party observers after purchase can support a trademark infringement claim.

positions.label: Point-of-sale confusion required
positions.summary: Holds that the relevant inquiry focuses on whether consumers are likely to be confused at the time of purchase, and post-sale confusion alone is insufficient.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
